utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning to everyone in and around this courtroom. Mr. Registrar, would you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case IT-09-92-T, the Prosecutor versus Ratko Mladic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber was informed that the OTP wants to raise a preliminary matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. There are actually two matters, as indicated yesterday, one of which was touched on briefly but I think may benefit from some additional clarification. That was with respect to MFI D920. I mentioned yesterday that the translation wasn't the issue but the question of whether or not the document had actually been raised during the course of the witness's testimony. And in that respect, I would note that the document was tendered on March 2nd at transcript page 32389. At that point, Mr. Lukic referred back to the previous day's session, noting that he had omitted to offer into evidence two documents. He referred to what became D919 by its exhibit number, 1D5364, and indeed that document was called up as under that exhibit number and discussed in court the previous day. And then he mentioned another one, as he put it, D5367. That then became MFI D920. Our search through the records of the previous day did not reveal a reference to 5367 or any discussion of that document and that's the issue at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic -- or if you want to further verify the transcripts, then we would like to hear from you after the break.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. We leave it to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And the second matter --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: I think -- I take it you referred to 1D5367.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: The 1 was missing.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I abbreviated the reference.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, which may cause some confusion and it suddenly looks like as if it's an exhibit, which it isn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And in fact, that's precisely what the transcript says when the document is mentioned on the 2nd, as I mentioned, when it was tendered. So we looked back for the reference under that number in the previous day's transcript without success. The second matter is one I presume the Court is aware of but did not want to simply assume, and that's with reference to the videolink motion for Witness -- proposed Witness Seselj. Yesterday the decision by the Appeals Chamber was issued effectively vacating or revoking the provisional release and ordering the Trial Chamber to revoke the previous order and order his return to the DU. It appears to us that essentially moots the motion pending before the Court, but I leave to the Court and to Mr. Lukic the precise mechanism for how that will be handled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: I think it's not in our hands anymore.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: No -- well, whether the motion has become moot and whether you withdraw it is in your hands, but whether the circumstances will develop in such a way that you finally have reasons to withdraw it -- I mean, a decision is one and then of course the decision has to be enforced.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: So our position is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- as long as the witness is not here, we cannot withdraw that -- our motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger relies on the legal situation at this moment, whereas the Defence apparently wants to rely at this moment on the situation practically. We'll think about that and of course we'll then hope that the practical situation ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We turn into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Registrar. The Chamber turned into private session because it wanted to verify whether it had touched upon anything related to the reasons for which the motion for a videolink was made confidential. It turned out that we have not touched upon any such thing, therefore the transcript can remain as it is. Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you, Mr. President. Let me just offer one additional observation, and that is the presumed dichotomy between the legal situation and the factual situation I think is not as clear as Mr. Lukic might have suggested. I think the -- that recent developments also impact on --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- the basis for the motion, any --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: -- possibility of enforcing any order, et cetera. So all those factors are also at play.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's the reason why we take our time to think about it and nothing is lost meanwhile. Anything else? I think there was a matter to be raised by the Defence, but you have decided to postpone that, Mr. Lukic, or was that the same matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: It is the same matter, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's the same --

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: -- I just have to receive the response from Mr. Traldi.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Then we will invite the witness to enter the courtroom. Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. I just wanted to alert the Trial Chamber that the next witness did receive a 90(E) admonishment and I also see that that admonishment is part of the uploaded transcript that might be offered pursuant to Rule 92 ter. Just for practical purposes, it might make sense then to admonish him at the outset.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Although he would have read the transcript then, but we'll certainly do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for the purposes of the record, Your Honour, the next witness is Edin Garaplija, whose appearance is compelled today by a subpoena issued by Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Good morning. Good morning, Mr. Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, before you give evidence, the Rules require that you make a solemn declaration, that you will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. The text is now handed out to you. May I invite you to make that solemn declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated, Mr. Garaplija. Mr. Garaplija, you'll be examined by Mr. Ivetic. You'll find Mr. Ivetic standing to your left. Mr. Ivetic is a member of the Defence team of Mr. Mladic, but before he starts his examination, I'd like to read to you - and it may not come as a surprise, I understand that it has been read to you before - I'll read to you Rule 90(E) of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence. The text is: "A witness may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate the witness. The Chamber may, however, compel the witness to answer the question. Testimony compelled in this way shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against the witness for any offence other than false testimony." Having read this Rule, where it says that you may object to making any statement which might tend to incriminate you, that you should address me if that situation arises and then you can address the Chamber and ask to be relieved from your duty to answer that question and then we'll decide on such a request. If that's clear to you, carefully listen to Mr. Ivetic's questions and please answer them. Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Good day, sir, can you please first state your full name for the record.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Good day. My name is Edin Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, you are appearing today before us pursuant to a subpoena that this Trial Chamber has issued compelling your attendance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I would like to call up 1D5308 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, what is being called up is a redacted transcript of your testimony in the Karadzic case on the 7th of February, 2013. Mr. Garaplija, have you had an opportunity to review the transcript of your Karadzic testimony which is before you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And do you stand by everything that you said in your prior testimony during the Karadzic trial as being correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If I were to ask you the same questions today, would your answers to those questions be substantially the same as recorded in the Karadzic transcript?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And pursuant to the solemn declaration that you have taken this morning, does that mean that the answers you would give, as in your Karadzic transcript, are truthful in nature?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, I would tender 1D5308 as the next Defence exhibit. We had originally not sought any of the associated documents, but in discussions with the Prosecution yesterday we agreed to tender 65 ter number 31931 which is referred to in the Karadzic transcript at page 13 through 15 as D2907.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That's correct, no objections.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Before we decide on admission, you said you reviewed the transcript. Do I understand that you can read the English language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Did you review it in English?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that additional information. Mr. Registrar, two exhibits to be assigned a number to -- the first is the extract of the testimony in the Karadzic case and the other one is the associated exhibit. The first one, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, 65 ter number 1D05308, the redacted excerpt of testimony will be Exhibit D980; and 65 ter number 31931 will be Exhibit D981.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: D980 and D981 are admitted into evidence. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, at this time I would read the witness summary as is customary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Edin Garaplija was a reserve member of the Ministry of the Interior of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina during the start of the war. From June 1992 onwards, he was a member of the State Security Service of the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. In June of 1996, he was deputy chief of the centre for the secret surveillance and leader of an anti-terrorist team, all within AID, the successor to the state security sector. He was tasked by AID director Kemal Ademovic to investigate the activities of Nedzad Herenda and the Seve unit. The Seve unit was established by Alija Delimustafic in April 1992 within the MUP of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina as a paramilitary unit of the State Security Service. The existence of this unit within the State Security Service of the MUP was kept a secret. One of the leaders of and later head of the State Security Service Mr. Nedzad Ugljen managed the work of the Seve unit. Mr. Ugljen was killed after the existence of this group became known, which was after the witness was arrested in an attempt to hide the investigation of the Seve group. Herenda was arrested and interviewed by the witness and Herenda confessed to his participation in the Seve unit and terrorist activities of the same, including sniping assassinations, setting explosives, et cetera. Among these activities was the killing of a French soldier in 1995 from the Executive Council building. Bosnian officials stated that the Serb side was responsible for the death of the French soldier shot while erecting anti-sniping barricades near the Holiday Inn. Herenda received payment of 2.000 marks for this killing. Another incident Herenda confessed to was the attempted assassination of General Sefer Halilovic which resulted in the killing of his wife and brother-in-law. The Seve group placed an explosive under the balcony or terrace of General Halilovic. The public was told that a shell launched by the Serb army, a Maljutka guided projectile had caused the killing and Herenda and the perpetrators left a Maljutka wire at the scene. Other crimes of the Seve unit included the liquidation of captured soldiers and civilians in the centre of Sarajevo committed personally by Herenda for which multiple witnesses were found as part of the investigation. Herenda also targeted Serbian women in Grbavica with a sniper rifle. The Seve unit further tried to murder by sniper fire Ismet Bajramovic, a commander of the BiH military police. Bajramovic was wounded and dislocated to another country for treatment. They were also involved in a shooting of two sentries during an attempted arrest of Musan Topalovic. After exposing the Seve group and their crimes, the witness was arrested and a show trial organised, in which the internal structures of the Bosnian forces of law enforcement and justice tried to hide under the carpet the existence of the Seve unit. Your Honours, that completes the summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garaplija, I would like to ask some additional questions. In the Karadzic transcript that has now been admitted as D980, at pages 6 through 7 of the same which relate to transcript pages 33384 through 33385, you talk about the Operation Eagle being undertaken upon the orders of Mr. Kemal Ademovic. Can you please tell us how it was that Mr. Ademovic approached you about the need to arrest Mr. Herenda?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Before I answer your question, I would have two objections to the statement -- to the statement summary that you have just read out. The first one relates to the passage referring to the murder of Nedzad Ugljen --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, the summary is not evidence. Even if there are imprecisions in there, the main purpose of it is to make the audience, to make the public, acquainted with what is approximately in your testimony so that they can follow any follow-up. It's not evidence itself, so if there are any inaccuracies we leave it then -- we, this Chamber, and the Prosecution will rely exclusively on what we find in the transcript of your testimony. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. But in fairness to the witness who is here via subpoena, perhaps I would ask that he be allowed to at least explain the differences --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I agree with you that since he was subpoenaed perhaps that he has an opportunity to -- not to add anything, but to just point at any inaccuracy in the summary. That means where the summary does not reflect your testimony. Nothing to add, nothing to alter. Please proceed. You may give your comments or corrections.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In the passage referring to the murder of Nedzad Ugljen, it is stated that Herenda's arrest was carried out to mask up the Seve unit's activities, but it was just the other way around. My second objection is that it is not Dusan Topalovic but Musan Topalovic, Caco.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for those corrections. Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Garaplija. Now can you tell us about how it was that Mr. Kemal Ademovic approached you about the need to arrest Mr. Herenda.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Having become director in the AID in Bosnia and Herzegovina which was the successor of the intelligence services of Bosnia-Herzegovina, Mr. Ademovic asked for a list of all active and reserve members of the agency. When one of his assistants, Nedzad Ugljen, provided a list of the Seve unit members to him, that one was curtailed, it was redacted, and that name was missing. And since at the beginning he was the commander of the Special Unit Bosna, he knew that Nedzad Herenda whose name was missing as a member of the Seve unit was responsible for the execution of the Serbian civilians in the park where the special unit of Bosnia-Herzegovina was located. When Ademovic saw that Nedzad Herenda's name was missing from the list, he gave me an order to start the Operation Eagle. Its objective was to find Nedzad Herenda, to collect evidence about his activities, and special emphasis was put on the fact that he was dangerous.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, do you recall what month and year that meeting took place where you received this task?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The meeting was held two months before my arrest in May 1996, so that the operation to locate and follow Nedzad Herenda started immediately after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: At that time, did Mr. Ademovic tell you anything further about the type of activities that Herenda was involved in for which he needed to be questioned?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I've already said this. He was suspected of heinous killing and liquidation of the captured civilians and soldiers in the park. That was the most incriminating information we had about Mr. Herenda. We learned about the rest after the interview with Nedzad Herenda when he was already under arrest.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, the orders that you had from Mr. Ademovic to arrest Mr. Herenda, were they memorialised in writing?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The initial order was verbal and then I got the order in writing.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us if any kind of difficulties were encountered when attempting to arrest Mr. Herenda?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The Seve unit was set up within the State Security Service as an independent organisation with very strong backing, so that the operation to locate and arrest Herenda had to be carried out in strict secrecy and nobody except the director, me as the leader of the team, and the operative officers who followed Herenda knew about it. Because we didn't know what the chain of command is, who within the service was operatively issuing orders to the Seve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, at the time of Herenda's arrest, was he in possession of any identity documents?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. He had an official ID. He had different passports in different names and he had an official police badge as well as special laissez-passer allowing him to move under the territory controlled by the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And, sir, just in terms of the laissez-passer, from which organ could such a document be obtained?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty which authority issued them and I'm not an expert to decide whether a passport is authentic or forged, so I can't answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did Herenda say anything about where he had obtained these identification documents from?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Throughout the interview, Herenda claimed that he was a legal member of the service and that the Seve unit was a legal unit set up within police structures, but as I've said before, it was a paramilitary unit installed at the beginning of the war when an agreement had been reached about joint army and police patrols and it was under the mandate of the then-Minister Alija Delimustafic. That unit was not under the regular system of command, nor did the legal leadership in the State Security Service know the membership of that unit or what they were doing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, could I seek verification -- further information about one of your previous answers. You said, when asked about the identity documents, you said: "He had different passports in different names ..." And one answer later you said: "I can't say with certainty which authority issued them and I'm not an expert to decide on whether" they are authentic or forged. But from what you saw, let's leave apart whether they were forged or not, from what you saw, who appeared to have issued those identity documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not go into the details of who issued these documents because we had only 72 hours under the law to conduct an interview with Nedzad Herenda, and we focused our investigation on the crimes committed by the Seve unit. So I'm not sure which agency, which organ issued these documents, but I know that normally it is the official police authorities that issue passports.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You said "several passports." Were they all BiH passports?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Two passports were BH passports. One was a normal civilian passport and another was official. Official passports are given to state officials when they go on official missions, and a third passport was, if I remember correctly, a Croatian one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. And the normal passport and the official passport, were they in different names?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot be sure now about the names on the passports. As I said, we didn't go into the details of these documents, and all that happened 20 years ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, though you remember it was under different names. I think earlier you said, but let me just look at that --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What did Herenda tell you about the original idea or mission of the Seve group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As I've stated before, Nedzad Herenda was convinced that all the missions of the Seve unit were legal, that is to say, approved by the official authorities. And through our investigation, we established that the Seve unit had two missions. One, conditionally speaking, was legal, it comprised legal tasks within the Ministry of the Interior such as providing security for VIPs and various consignments that were dispatched to or from Sarajevo; and the second prong was dirty business, so to speak, and that was handled by the renegade members of the Seve unit, including Herenda, by the exiled ones, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And these dirty -- this dirty business that you've identified, was it aimed at any particular groups or entities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just raise to express a concern about -- so we have some clarity in the transcript. I see that Mr. Ivetic's question clearly asked about a conversation aspect, what did Herenda tell the witness; and the witness then moved through our investigation into other matters. So I believe we're starting to get a less-clear foundation or area as to the basis of this witness's knowledge. I just wanted to raise that concern that -- before the answers get too complex.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Ivetic, I take it that you're also trying to make as clear as possible what the witness learned from his conversations with Herenda and what he may have learned through other sources during his investigation. Witness, that's important for this Chamber to know and Mr. Ivetic will consider that when formulating his questions. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: With the advice of the Trial Chamber, I would then ask you, sir, what did Herenda state to you during the interview about who or what was targeted as part of the dirty business that he -- that you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I just object, leading. I mean, I think this came up in his last testimony too, the questions were quite often phrased, what did Herenda tell you about X, introducing the topic, as opposed to just eliciting what the conversation was and what was told. And now we have an inference that this was what was said, but that has not -- actually that fact has not been established yet that that was what was told to the witness by Herenda.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let me just re-read that. Mr. Ivetic, any response?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I thought I was responding to the testimony of the witness prior, but it's off my screen right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The witness said something about dirty business and then your question was -- well, as a matter of fact: Did he tell you whether, and if so, what the target was of such dirty business.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's what you would like to know. Dirty business, if you say, well, you never know where there's a target for dirty business, that's theoretically true, but practically you may proceed, Mr. Ivetic. Could you answer that question, whether there was any -- whether you were told that there was any specific target; and if so, what that target was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Seve unit had specific targets, but they also had the freedom to act independently, at least that's what Nedzad Herenda told us during his interview. The specific targets have been named in this summary and they included the highest -- the top officials, such as UNPROFOR members, when Herenda confessed that he had shot at an UNPROFOR member in the city centre; and the officials of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, including the Chief of Staff, Mr. Sefer Halilovic. He was one of the targets. Herenda also admitted to a number of other crimes beginning with the crime that he committed in the big park when he executed a group of captured members of the Serbian army as well as a number of civilians after the crime, when he did target practice shooting at civilians or, as he called them, the women in black because he was convinced at that time that those were Serb women. So the unit had both specific targets and the freedom to choose their own targets in certain cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'd like to now focus a little more on the shooting of the French soldier which is discussed at page 9 of your Karadzic transcript, which corresponds to transcript page 33387 of the same. Did the operation against the French soldier -- did Herenda tell you what the objective of the same was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The purpose of that action was to blame the Serbian side, and Herenda chose a place which was in the line of vision of Serb snipers in the city centre. That's how he chose his position.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And according to what he told you, did the operation against the French soldier go as planned?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: In executing that action, he shot the French soldier dead and then a number of officials said that the French soldier had been hit from Serb territory. So it was a successful cover-up and the Serb side was blamed for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at page -- I think it's 12 of your transcript, which is 33390, at lines 4 through 8, you indicate that Herenda received amounts to the tune of thousands of German marks for these actions. Did -- what was your understanding of who paid him or where this money was coming from for his activities?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I can't say with certainty who paid Herenda. He claimed that he received money for the perpetration of some crimes and the amounts were in the thousands of German marks.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in page 3 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you say, "I can't say with certainty who paid" him, why do you say, "I can't say with certainty"? Did you hear rumours? Did you hear anything from Mr. Herenda? Did he tell you anything about it, although you could not verify that? Could you tell us what you learned as -- and how you learned what the possible sources of that payment may have been.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Herenda always cited Nedzad Ugljen as the person issuing him with orders. Nedzad Ugljen was one of the leaders of the service, and I suppose he gave him orders and named certain targets and paid him money. Herenda had contact only with his superior and never mentioned that anyone else ever issued him orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, at page 34 of your transcript which is transcript page 33413, you mention Musan Topalovic, whom we have also discussed today -- pardon me, it's page 35 of the underlying transcript. And I wanted to ask you, first of all: Did Mr. Topalovic have a nickname?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. His nickname was Caco.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And at the time what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could you repeat the number as it appears on the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It should be transcript page 33413, which ought to be page 35 of the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And it's lines 4 through 9, I believe.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you for that information.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Was the name Caco or Celo? In the transcript it says "Celo."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Musan -- Musan Topalovic was nicknamed Caco, whereas Celo was a man called Ismet Bajramovic, nicknamed Celo, and he was another of Herenda's targets.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I believe, Your Honours, we see that at lines 13 through 14 of the Karadzic transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Garaplija, did Mr. Musan Topalovic have a position that he held at the time of the conflict with -- where the Herenda group became involved?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. Musan Topalovic was at that time commander of the brigade in the surrounded Sarajevo, the brigade of the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: From your discussions with Mr. Herenda, was there any discussion of how this encounter with the sentries at Musan Topalovic's location came about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: During his interview, Herenda said clearly that their mission was to hit the guards outside the command of Musan Topalovic, and to do that specifically at a time when a team of inspectors had entered the command in order to take Topalovic to an investigating interview, because he was suspected of certain crimes. At the same time, Herenda's colleagues from the Seve unit also shot at different positions of the joint forces that were supposed to support this team of inspectors so that in those early moments they faked mutual conflict and both sides fell for it, unfortunately. So there were many casualties; namely, the entire team of inspectors that had entered the command of Musan Topalovic was brutally killed, and on the other hand, joint forces liquidated a number of the members of Topalovic's brigade. This crisis in the city centre lasted several hours, and then Topalovic was forced to surrender. He was then taken to the command of the BH army corps and shortly after was killed in an attempt to escape.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Did your investigative team develop any theory as to why the Seve group had been tasked to do what they did, to fake mutual combat?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Objection, calls for speculation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That objection is denied. The question is whether a theory was developed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, maybe I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: This is a question of fact. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am not speculating right now about these events. All these events have been documented. A lot has been said, both at trials and in the media, about this, and as I said before Nedzad Herenda provided us with information from inside the Seve unit --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, let me stop you there. The question was whether the investigative team, that is, the investigative team at the time, developed any theory about why the group had been tasked to do what they did. So we're not asking you at this moment to analyse what you may have learned at trials later, but did at the time the investigative group develop such theory? Perhaps you could first tell us whether they did or not.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Our task was not to come up with theories; it was to document crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Whether it was your task or not, the question simply is whether you did develop at the time a theory, yes or no. If not, then we'll move on and perhaps questions will be put to you about what the investigations revealed apart from any developed theory. Did you develop such a theory at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed, Mr. Ivetic. Well, when I say that --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- I should have first looked at the clock. Could you tell us where we are in terms of time, Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, I believe approximately 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: 30 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, you may follow the usher. We take a break of some 20 minutes. We'd like to see you back after that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take a break and resume at five minutes to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If you're ready, Mr. Ivetic, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, during your interview of Mr. Herenda, did he discuss anything about the purpose of the Seve group's creating a fake conflict between the two sides during the arrest of Musan Topalovic, Caco?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: In every crime committed by the Seve group, you can follow the same pattern. The purpose was to create as much conflict as possible and to spill as much blood on both sides.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, at page 33 of the Karadzic transcript which should correlate to transcript page 33411, at lines 11 through 25 you identify the cases that we've talked about, and then at lines -- in relation to attacks by the Seve unit against Bosnian Muslims. And then you say at line 22 through 25: "These are the two cases that I heard about in my interview and investigation of Nedzad Herenda, but since more than 17 years have passed, I do not exclude a possibility that there were other cases. I could have mentioned other cases in my interview with the OTP." First of all, can you tell us when it was that you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: In the year 2000. I sent an appeal to the organisation for human rights and one letter to The Hague Tribunal. After that I was contacted by the investigators of The Hague Tribunal, and they then talked to me for several days.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And now do you recall any other instances of the Seve group targeting persons from Sarajevo, including Muslims, that were discovered by you as part of your investigation and that you may have talked about with the OTP during your interview, apart from these instances from the Karadzic testimony that we have now gone through?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: In the Karadzic case I answered very specific questions. When it comes to other cases, at the beginning of today's testimony I said that Herenda told me that he had committed several crimes consisting of opening sniper fire on civilians, both on the Bosnian side as well as on the Serb side. He opened sniper fire on Grbavica and on the Vrbanja Bridge, more specifically. For a time they secured the bridge on Grbavica. Today the bridge is known as the Bridge of Suada Dilberovic and before the war it was the Vrbanja Bridge. They killed a couple. And the second sniping incident that you have reminded me of was the attempt to execute Ismet Bajramovic, Celo, who was the commander of the military police at the time in the surrounded Sarajevo. I suppose he would have been a most unpleasant witness of certain events. Celo survived the murder attempt, although he was shot straight in the heart, very professionally. However, his life was saved by doctors and then he was moved to a third country for further treatment. I believe that he was moved to Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we could focus to the actions at the Vrbanja Bridge, first of all, you said for a time they secured the bridge on Grbavica. Could you please give us what more details you have as to what they -- what the securing of the bridge was in relation to, what other activities of the Seve unit.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Although the war lasted from 1992 to 1995, all the sides were involved in the trading business amongst themselves. Certain activities, for example, the exchanges of civilians, took place at certain points such as the Vrbanja Bridge. What was traded there were lots of different commodities, including weapons and drugs that were then brought to Sarajevo which was surrounded.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to the activities of the Seve at the bridge, the Vrbanja Bridge, you indicated a couple had been killed. Did you have any more information as to the ethnicity of that couple?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. They were known as the Romeo and Juliet of Sarajevo. The man was a Serb and the woman was a Bosniak. They had a lot of money on themselves and they tried to escape surrounded Sarajevo and get to the Serbian side across the bridge. Herenda, together with his colleague Dragan from the Seve unit, actually targeted that couple and hit them and killed them. The position from which they opened fire was a couple of hundred metres away as you're looking from the side of the city to the left, that's where the building of the school of electrical engineering was. It was known as Steleks. From there, Herenda opened fire -- actually, he hit the couple from a sniper.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could we ask again whether this is what you learned from Herenda or that you -- are there reports written about this or what's the source of your knowledge?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We learned that from Herenda himself during the interview in June 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, any other source of knowledge apart from hearing this from Herenda?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at that moment. However, it was covered by the media after that. Over the past several years there have also been some TV shows about that; before that, newspapers covered the story quite excessively.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But, Mr. Ivetic, needless to say that you then have to know where the media got their information from, but please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can go back to the time-period when this couple was shot on the bridge. Who was blamed for it at that time-period, during the war?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Like for a majority of sniping activity, it was the Serbian side that was blamed for that. To be more precise, during the war nobody was aware of the existence of the Seve unit. We learned about them only after the war, in 1996.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And you identified in your answer that Herenda worked with a colleague named Dragan. To your knowledge, was this individual, Dragan, ever arrested or punished for his deeds as part of the Seve group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Interestingly enough, Dragan Bozic, who was a prominent member of the Seve unit, and Nedzad Herenda mentioned him a lot in his statement, he also used the name Dragan Sosic, he was never put on trial. As far as I know, he is still employed at the Central Bank of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Although his name is mentioned often, I mentioned it in several of my statements given both to the local as well as international institutions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, could I seek clarification of one of the previous answers. You were asked who was blamed for this killing and you said it was the Serbian side that was blamed. Blamed by whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I've already told you, the media and official reports always asserted that sniping of Sarajevo came either from Grbavica or from the surrounding hilltops. I can't give you an answer about this specific case as to which of the media published it or which of the officials stated it, but in general terms, all the sniping incidents, all the sniping fire opened on Sarajevo was ascribed to the Serbian side.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Now, did the Serbian media do the same, to say the Serbs are to be blamed for all this; or did they rather blame the other side for sniping or even sniping at their own people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I know, the Serbian media said the opposite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In other words, they claimed that the other side was responsible for sniping. It was a period when everybody blamed the other side for the things that were happening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So when you were asked who was blamed for it, the answer is that, as usual, the one party blamed the other party, rather than Serbs to be blamed for it because the Serbs would blame the other party for it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now I want to fast-forward to the circumstances just before your arrest. At page 6 through 7 of the Karadzic transcript which should correlate to transcript pages 33385 through -6, you briefly say that you were arrested and a rigged show trial was held. Can you tell me of how and when you first were told that you were to be arrested?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: After Nedzad Herenda was wounded in an escape attempt and hospitalised, where his wounds were tended to, my colleague from the service, Fikret Masic, conveyed a message to me and the message was that in order to appease the general public there would be arrests. I and my team were to be arrested. Because everything had gone too far, as he told me at the time. After such a long time I can only say that at the moment when the order was issued to launch Eagle, the director did not know what crimes the Seve unit had been involved in. And when he learned that from us, i.e., when he saw it in Herenda's statement, he himself decided that it would be better for everything to be hushed up. We would then become scapegoats, we would be arrested and put on a rigged trial. I'm not excluding the possibility that somebody had ordered him to do that, and I'm talking about Director Ademovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a colleague Fikret Masic. What was his position at the time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: At the time, Masic was the chief of the counter-intelligence section in the AID.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what did Mr. Masic tell you was going to happen during your trial?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: He told us to take it easy, to hand over all the documents to him, and that he, i.e., the service and its director, Ademovic, would make sure that we would only spend a few days in the investigation prison and that we would all be free to go after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What did he tell you about defence attorneys for you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: When I was remanded in custody, Fahrija Karkin, an attorney, came to me and told me that he had been sent by Director Ademovic. He gave me a code and that's how I knew that he had been sent on the instructions of Director Ademovic. I accepted him as my lawyer; however, it turned out later that he was the one who was charged with rigging the investigation and the trial that would be conducted against me and my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And what, if anything, did Mr. Masic tell you about the judges for the trial?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Masic also told me that the judges were all in the cahoots and that they would be very inclined to set us free. All it took was a little time for the entire situation to calm down and to hush up the very existence of the Seve group.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: What instructions did Mr. Fikret Masic give you in relation to the documentation from your investigation of Herenda?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: We handed over the entire documentation to Masic, I'm talking about our record of the Herenda interview. Masic was very categorical when he instructed us that if there was anything left, that it had to be destroyed and burned. He ordered me that in the trial we should keep quiet, that we should not mention the service director, and the Eagle order, and particularly that we shouldn't mention anything that we had learned from Herenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you please give us a chronology and more details about what actually transpired after your arrest and during the trial?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: From the moment we were arrested until the moment we were finally released from prison, five years lapsed. I and two of my colleagues were arrested and charged with the kidnapping of Nedzad Herenda, of ill-treating him, and finally that we attempted to kill him. In that trial we kept quiet, we did not say anything in our defence, because we were convinced that, as Masic and Ademovic told us, the service would talk to the judges who controlled the trial and that we would finally be set free. However, all the time the charges against us were -- we were being set up through the lawyer that was supposed to defend us, and we turned out to be criminals and Nedzad Herenda was portrayed as a model citizen and even a hero by some media. The banality of the trial and the way it was staged was acknowledged by the Court of Human Rights. When I realised that I was eventually sentenced to 14 years in prison and after I myself had survived two attempts of murder within the prison, I sent an appeal to the institution for human rights. There were six foreign judges on the panel and the president of that panel was Judge Michele Picard. I sent an appeal and in my appeal, I provided all the details and also that I was never given the right to appeal against my judgement, which was a gross violation of my human rights. The Court of Human Rights voted in my favour. The six foreign judges over-voted the six local judges appointed by the three ruling parties. They agreed to confirm my sentence. In other words, the court judged in our favour and sent the whole case for re-trial. However, when we were brought to the Supreme Court, after a certain while I realised that the re-trial was also rigged because I recognised one of the judges of whom Masic said that he was the service's associate. In his introductory statement, that judge said that the formal rights and requirements had been met because we were brought to court but we were not allowed to say anything in our defence. That's when I realised that the trial would be rigged and that nothing would be different. At that moment a person approached me, a man of whom I'd never heard before, I'd never seen him before, he introduced himself to me as a lawyer from The Hague Tribunal. Later I met him and I learned that his name was Carl Kenning, he was one of the investigators who had previously interviewed me. He told me that he had heard everything and he had seen it with his own eyes and that that would not be the end of the violation of my human rights and that he would report back to The Hague Tribunal. And then an unprecedented thing happened. I was brought for the third time before the Supreme Court. I was then allowed to mount my defence and to lodge an official document on Operation Eagle. That's when my sentence was altered and I was sentenced to the time already served in prison; in other words, I was sentenced for some lesser crimes. Soon thereafter, we were all released, first myself and then my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: When was Mr. Nedzad Ugljen killed?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Soon after our arrest, perhaps two months into custody, i.e., two months into isolation because we were not allowed any contacts with the outer world. We did not have access to newspapers or any other media. Our only contact was through the lawyer that had been assigned to us. From one of the guards who guarded us, I learned that Nedzad Ugljen had been killed as an unwelcome witness of all the happenings and the activities of the Seve group as well as the events surrounding the rigging of my process -- my trial and the trial of my colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: To your knowledge, was anyone ever arrested or charged with the killing of Mr. Ugljen?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know, nobody was ever charged or arrested for Ugljen's killing, although he was involved in the police and security missions of highest order before the war and during the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, apart from your interview in the year 2000 to the Office of the Prosecutor and your testimony in the Karadzic case in 2013, did you give any other statements to judicial organs about the things you have testified here about today?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes. I provided statements to local courts, i.e., to the cantonal prosecutor's office in Sarajevo, that was very quickly after my release from prison, as well as several statements to the authorised police organs who contacted me after my turned for redress to the Court of Human Rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, your estimate was 30 minutes, I think, before the break. We are at that point approximately now. Could you tell us --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: One question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: One question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, my final question: What is your motive for talking publicly about the events relating to Mr. Herenda and the Seve group and testifying now at two trials about the activities of Herenda and the Seve group?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The Seve group, according to all that I learned, followed the same pattern of development like other paramilitary groups on all sides, including the Red Berets. Its objective and goal was to spill as much blood as possible and to blame each other as much as possible in order to make life together impossible and to inflict as much destruction as possible. And my only motive is for those who committed crimes to be charged with those crimes instead of those crimes being ascribed to other people.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, I have no more questions for you. I thank you for both your time and your testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Witness, I have one follow-up question which is directly related to the last question that was put to you by Mr. Ivetic. You told us what your motive was for talking publicly about these events. What then explains that you wanted to be subpoenaed before appearing before this Court? Why didn't you voluntarily meet the request of the Defence to come and testify?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the answer to your question is rather simple. All the media in Sarajevo and in Bosnia knew when the Karadzic and Mladic Defence called me to testify, and I don't know how they knew, but even before I got official documentation that I should appear, the media reported that I was invited by the Defence of criminals Karadzic and Mladic and that I was about to testify in their defence, to help them, which is not true. I'm not here to defend anyone or to help them. I responded both times to the invitation of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but you insisted on that. You didn't meet the request by the Defence and you could have publicly stated that even though called by the Defence, that you would be a witness of the truth and therefore it doesn't matter whether you're called by the one party or by the other. Why did you insist on being subpoenaed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I never insisted. Both times the Defence teams contacted me, asking me to come voluntarily as a witness, and I refused. And this is documented in writing. And then the subpoena was issued at the request of the Defence team. I didn't even know what a subpoena was until I got one.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Then the same question. Why did you refuse if you say: This is what I want, to tell publicly about the events? Under those circumstances, especially if you wouldn't know what a subpoena would be, the logic would be that you say: This is what I wish, so therefore if they invite me I'll do it, rather than to refuse. That's what we're trying to understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't refuse to come. I gave my statement to OTP investigators 15 years ago, in 2000, and I stand by that statement today --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: A second ago you said you were invited to come voluntarily and you refused. So to say that you didn't refuse is -- "both times the Defence teams contacted me, asking me to come voluntarily as a witness, and I refused ..." So to say one line later that you didn't refuse comes a bit as a surprise. Any further comments on what I just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps I misspoke. When I said "refused," I didn't mean refused to make a statement, but refusing to be a Defence witness. I mentioned that all the media had ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you for those answers. Mr. Weber, are you ready to cross-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, you'll now be cross-examined by Mr. Weber. You'll find Mr. Weber to your right. Mr. Weber is counsel for the Prosecution. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Garaplija.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The information that you have recounted in your previous testimony and in court today about the Seve group, those were things Mr. Herenda supposedly told you in June of 1996; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your interview of Mr. Herenda occurred between the afternoon of 25 June 1996 and lasted until the morning of 29 June 1996; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct. Under the law of the agency --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: -- for investigation and documentation, we had 72 hours --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll move rather quickly through things today, so I will go through them. Mr. Herenda was not free to go during this time?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's right, he was arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Meaning he was in your custody?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You'd never had a conversation with Nedzad Herenda before you took him into custody on the 25th of June, 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Not about the activities of the Seve unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Are you saying that you had talked to Nedzad Herenda before the 25th of June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: No, I never talked to him before, but I had seen him around the building of the headquarters of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: When you took him into custody, you took Mr. Herenda to a secret location between the 25th and the 29th of June; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did not bring him into your headquarters or process Mr. Herenda for any charges; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I've said earlier that it was a secret operation and we didn't know who else within the service was involved, that's why we chose a secret location to interview him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You did not bring him into your headquarters or process Mr. Herenda for any charges; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: To the best of your knowledge, the Seve group consisted of approximately ten people at the beginning of the war and possibly grew to about 30 people by the end of the war; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's the total number of the Seve unit, but the number of men responsible for the crimes I've mentioned was much smaller, it was three to five.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, the previous answer is not absolutely clear. The "no" could relate to your question "right?" or the sentence before that. You should clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, thank you very much. And I'll just break it up.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, I'm going back to a question that I asked you and I'll just separate it. When you took Mr. Herenda into custody, you did not bring him into your headquarters; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: No, we did not bring him to the headquarters of the service. We brought him instead to a location that was also a base of the service.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Herenda was not processed for any charges; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: We filed no criminal complaint against Herenda because it was not our job. Our job was only to collect information. Criminal complaints are only filed by our leaders, by our superiors.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber has received a portion of your testimony in the Karadzic case. I'd like to ask you a more broad question that relates to your entire Karadzic testimony. Were all of your answers throughout your entire Karadzic testimony truthful and accurate?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Sitting here, I can't guarantee that every sentence was recorded exactly as I said it, but everything that concerns the Seve unit, in that part my testimony is absolutely truthful and accurate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, Witness, whether it was recorded exactly as you said, that is something we can verify because we have the audio of your testimony. The question simply is: Did at any point, did you not tell the truth when you testified in the Karadzic case? And don't worry about how it was recorded.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the Prosecutor means the information I provided about the second-instance trial in the agency for human rights, I supplemented that testimony, saying that the trial judgement was not in our favour, but the appeals judgement was. I would like to know if that's what the Prosecutor meant in his question. As for the rest of my evidence, I maintain that it is correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I don't know whether that's a specific concern to you, Mr. Weber, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I was asking him a broad --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just at this stage I was asking him a broad question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: So apart from -- did you tell the truth when you testified in Karadzic? That's the simple question. Or is there any point where you say, well, it may -- I may not have told the truth or not the whole truth?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my testimony in the Karadzic case, I was telling the truth, but there is a moment when I was explaining my position and my appeal to the Court of Human Rights. I had two suits before the Court of Human Rights, once when I was in custody, that was -- that judgement was not in my favour; the other one when I was freed was in my favour. That's the only thing that was in dispute with the Prosecution, but I didn't make any mistakes and didn't overlook anything in my testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to that for the time being. Mr. Weber, I leave it in your hands.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And just so we have clarification, in the Karadzic case, you discussed the criminal proceedings related to your detention of Nedzad Herenda in June 1996; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I have a few questions before -- for context before we look at your previous testimony, and I know you've touched on some of these today already. After Herenda's interview in June of 1996, you were arrested for mistreating Nedzad Herenda while you had him in custody; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's what the trumped-up indictment said, that we had been arrested for the attempt to murder and kidnap Nedzad Herenda.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The specific charges that were initially brought against you were abduction and attempted murder; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Charges related to Mr. Herenda's custody were also brought against two of your associates, Haris Pezo, P-e-z-o, and Refik Muran; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Pezo and Mr. Muran were with you during the detention of Mr. Herenda; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, and not only them but two other operatives who were involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Just so we keep on going with the proceedings here, the BiH State Court initially convicted you and your associates for the abduction and attempted murder of Mr. Herenda; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's not true. We were convicted by the Cantonal Court of Sarajevo as a lower court, and the Supreme Court of the Federation in these bogus proceedings made their judgement. And after the proceedings before the Court of Human Rights, there were two more appearances before the Supreme Court --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm just trying to have it clear before we lump all the proceedings together. You were initially convicted by the cantonal court for abduction and attempted murder; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's right. We were convicted of abduction and attempted murder while we chose to remain silent.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, going onward, after the proceedings before the BiH Supreme Court and the Human Rights Chamber, the charge of abduction was overturned and your convictions were upheld for the crimes of attempted murder and maltreatment in the discharge of duty; right? That was the final outcome of what you were convicted for?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: There is no Supreme Court of Bosnia-Herzegovina. There is only the Supreme Court of the Federation, and it's before that court that we fought our legal battle. And there were two trials. After the second time and after the involvement of The Hague Tribunal, the verdict reduced our sentence and some counts were dismissed. The remaining count was abuse of authority, that is to say, attempted murder. So the sentence was reduced from 14 years to seven. And after that, they granted me clemency, as they put it, so they released me immediately after I've served five years, one month, and one day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I'm about to get into some materials. I don't know -- I know it's a minute or two early but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We are close to the time where we would take a break.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: We'll take that break now. The witness may follow the usher. I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I already announced that after the break, on from ten minutes to 1.00, I'll be unable to sit and my colleagues will decide whether or not they'll continue to hear the case in my absence, which will be of short duration, that is, only the remainder of this day. We take a break and we resume at quarter past 12.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: While we're waiting for the witness to be escorted into the courtroom, I would briefly deal with a matter unrelated to that. It's about the Rule 92 ter motion for Nikola Erceg. The Chamber notes that on the 15th of September, 2014, the Defence filed a motion tendering 55 associated exhibits with Witness Nikola Erceg. On the 28th of March, 2015, the Defence sent the Chamber a revised list of exhibits containing 60 associated exhibits, including 11 exhibits which have already been admitted into evidence. Pursuant to the Chamber's guide-lines, the Chamber hereby invites the Defence to consider reducing the number of associated exhibits by, for example, tendering some of these documents with the witness during examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, if I may, the Prosecution will be calling up Exhibit D980, page 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I believe Exhibit D980 is actually on the screen. If I could please have page 8 of that document. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, this is part of your previous testimony in the Karadzic case. On this page at the top you stated: "And only after two years of serving sentences -- these sentences we were given, I addressed the International Court for Human Rights which had a branch office in Bosnia-Herzegovina. It was called the Human Rights Hall, presided by a French Judge, Michele Picard. Our judgement was rendered null and void by that human rights court and a judge rapporteur, Giovanni Grasso. This court ordered a re-trial, following which we were released from prison and pardoned in some way." This was not a true statement since the judgement was not rendered null and void; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I said a moment ago the verdict was not quashed, it was only requalified so that we received practically the sentence that we had already served. It's true that in 2008 we made our first appeal before the Human Rights Chamber --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: 1998.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And that process took eight years, so that the judgement was made only in 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you could please focus on my question. You've given explanations for this a couple times already. This statement that you gave in the Karadzic case was not true, your judgement was not rendered null and void?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The judgement of the Supreme Court of the Federation was quashed and there was a re-trial, I've already explained that, and there were in fact two re-trials. The first time, a lawyer from The Hague was involved and looked into that first re-trial and found deficiencies, so there was a new re-trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you're giving explanations again. Just really simple: Are you saying that this answer was the truth or are you acknowledging that this answer was not the truth?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That answer was not incomplete, but it's truthful. Now I gave a complete answer and explained how it all went.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31925, e-court page 26.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is another part of your testimony in the Karadzic case. It was a portion that was not tendered by the Defence, and before I ask you any questions about this extra material: Prior to your testimony today, did you review your entire Karadzic transcript or just the excerpts that were provided to you?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I reviewed what the Defence team gave me.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Were there portions of that transcript that were redacted or had black markings over it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Well, I cannot be precise about this, whether there were or weren't redactions, I mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. I'd like to direct you to line 12 of this page --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But before we continue. Witness, when was it that you reviewed your Karadzic transcript?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After arriving last Friday, I reviewed the transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You must have noticed whether there were thick black -- blackened-out portions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I didn't pay attention to the details. I wasn't so careful. I don't rule out the possibility that there were some blacked-out portions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: If I would show you from a distance how that looks like, could you then -- would that refresh your memory whether you found any such thing in the -- and I show to the witness at this moment page 33401 at a distance of some 5, 6 metres. Is this what you saw?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, there was no such thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Could you assist us, Mr. Ivetic, as to whether the witness was given the -- and I showed him this just for you to know as well. Even from a distance you can see that you hardly can miss the blackened-out portions. Did you show the witness the redacted version or did you show the witness the unredacted version?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We had both with us and I don't know which one the witness had. I also had with me a copy of the recording of the audio, which he did not say he needed because there was already a recording on YouTube of the B/C/S audio of the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, but if you're seeking the attestation of a witness, wouldn't it be good to know exactly what he reviewed so we know exactly what he attested to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, we've had this procedure with the Prosecution witnesses where I made exactly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, I'm --

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- that same point as Your Honour, and Your Honour told me that's the wrong way to do it. So I'm a little confused as to what the right way is. We've had witnesses from the Prosecution that have listened to the entirety of their testimony and then only a portion of that testimony has been brought in by the Prosecution. I objected to one such witness and you overruled that objection, Your Honour. So I'm confused now as to what the procedure is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think, as a matter of fact, you're referring to audio, aren't you?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: I think I asked the witness whether he had reviewed the written version and whether what is true for the audio, where it's difficult just to cut out the relevant portions, whereas in writing that's different. But as a matter of fact, I didn't ask you whether you were unhappy with any previous ruling, but you apparently think that it's -- when seeking the attestation on the basis of a written transcript, that you would say it's not relevant to know what exactly the witness attested to in terms of what was shown to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's not what I'm saying, Your Honour. I'm saying that we had an instance where it was my understanding that the Prosecution had wanted to present part of the transcript for their case, the cross-examination, and had suggested to lead that with the witness and I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. That's not an answer to my question because my question was: Wouldn't it be good to know exactly what he reviewed so we know exactly what he attested to? That was my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Not whether you disagreed with any previous ruling. Could I receive an answer to that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think I gave that answer --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- I said "yes, Your Honour," about two lines ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Let's leave it to that. Please proceed, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, directing your attention to the page before you, which is transcript page 33404 in the Karadzic proceedings, you were asked: "Okay. And you referred in your direct examination to your arrest and conviction following this interview with Herenda. Just to be precise, you were arrested specifically for the mistreatment of Herenda in the course of the interview, in particular abduction, maltreatment in discharge of duty, and attempted murder; right?" Your answer: "Yes.
