That was a bogus indictment that was quashed later before the Human Rights Hall, and the domestic judicial institutions were ordered to conduct a re-trial where a verdict, a conviction, was handed down for overstepping official authority and the unlawful imprisonment that we endured, one year, one month, and one day. After that, I personally instituted another proceedings before the Human Rights Hall that resulted in the quashing of the entire judgement, and I have since never been tried for anything." Mr. Garaplija, this answer was untrue because the Human Rights Chamber did not quash the entire judgement; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Correct. This is a mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir --

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: -- I've not seen this before and when I spoke about --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'll read on. You were next asked, and this continues on to the next page: "Q. Well, in fact, Mr. Garaplija, what you've just described is untrue. You were initially convicted, as you say. Your case did go before the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber in 2000. They did find a violation of your rights. There were then further proceedings at the Bosnian Supreme Court in 2000 where they quashed the conviction for abduction, maintained the conviction for mistreatment in discharge of duty and attempted murder, and then you brought a further application to the Bosnian Human Rights Chamber, and, in 2002, that chamber found that there had been no violation of your rights in the 2000 Bosnian Supreme Court judgement that had convicted you for mistreatment and discharge of duty and attempted murder. That's actually what happened, isn't it?" Your answer: "That's precisely what I said, except I didn't mention ... in the second proceedings I was found guilty of overstepping my official authorities, not attempted murder. So the abduction and attempted murder did not feature in the appeals proceedings. And shortly afterward, I was released from the state prison." Just stopping here before I read on, during this specific answer in your Karadzic testimony, you are acknowledging that you did not provide complete information to the court; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: If you look at this just as a mistake as the second trial only -- but if you look at -- then it's correct. But if you look at the whole chronology, then you can see that I'm basing my words on the judgement of the Human Rights Chamber, after which my sentence was altered and I was released. I'm talking about two trials before the Human Rights Chamber. The first one resulted in this: The panel of six judges judged in our favour, in favour of our appeal. This is what saved our lives, this is what is important, and as a result, we were released and I'm able to sit before you today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: All right. Let's read on. Next question: "Well, in your earlier answer you had said that in the second proceedings before the Human Rights Chamber, that those proceedings resulted in the quashing of the entire judgement. That's entirely false. That Human Rights Chamber decision upheld your conviction; right?" You answered: "That is correct. Perhaps I told it wrong, but I said I was never again tried in this case. That's what I meant." Sir, the fact is that you did not provide truthful testimony about the outcome of the proceedings against you; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Not correct. In the second proceedings I asked for compensation and for the quashing of the sentence. The second sentence was conducted after we were released from prison and our appeal was not accepted, i.e., there was no trial. No court was ordered to conduct a trial. But very soon after that appeal, the Human Rights Chamber was disbanded as well as its participation in the Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina and in the prosecutor's office of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: During your previous testimony you were also shown the final 2002 decision by the Human Rights Chamber; correct? You remember that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: You are talking about the year 2002. This is the second decision. And I, on the other hand, am talking about the first decision which was passed in the year 2000, hence the misunderstanding. That's why we are talking at cross-purposes. I've just tried to explain to you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: First of all, slow down. Second, you were asked whether during your previous testimony you were also shown the final 2002 decision by the Human Rights Chamber. Was that shown to you during that testimony or was that not shown to you? Or don't you remember?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't remember that it was shown, but it was mentioned as the second decision in my case. And when you look at the year, you can see that it was the second decision because the first was passed in the year 2000 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: You don't remember, that's an answer to my question. Mr. Weber will put further questions to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the proceedings before the Human Rights Chamber in -- that was eventually decided in 2002, you made claims you could not support; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: What claims do you have in mind, Mr. Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm asking you a broad question. Before that chamber --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: At such an abstract level, Mr. Weber, that you should specify what claims you had on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Well, one of the unsupported claims you made before the Human Rights Chamber was that a Supreme Court judge was collaborating with the Bosnian secret service to frame you for the mistreatment of Herenda in 1996. That was one of your claims; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct, and I did say that about Judge Malik Hadziomerovic [as interpreted] who was a judge rapporteur. And after the observations made by the lawyer from The Hague Tribunal, he was withdrawn from that trial and he did not appear as one of the judges during my third re-trial. The judge's name was Malik Hadziomerovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I put it to you that that wasn't the case and actually the claims that you made related to this judge were unsupported before the Human Rights Chamber?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I don't know what is the basis of your claim that this is not correct, but I told you that Fikret Masic has told me that that judge was responsible for our liberation and that never materialised. Based on that statement --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the --

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: -- I asked for the exclusion of that judge.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I understand you asked for it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Let's look at 65 ter 31923.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the 12 April 2002 Human Rights Chamber decision. We see the panel that it was delivered by and it's signed by Judge Picard. The full procedural history of your proceedings before the BiH Supreme Court and Human Rights Chamber are contained in this decision so I'm not going to discuss them further with you. Seeing this document, do you recall having seen this during your previous testimony?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, I'm familiar with the document. In 2002, when I was already free, it was handed to me after the session of this panel together with the separate opinion of Judge Giovanni Grasso, which was a dissenting opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Directing your attention to paragraph 51 that states: "The applicant's representative, in answer to the Chamber's request, stated that he had challenged one of the judges in the renewed appellate proceedings because he is allegedly a collaborator with the secret service ..." I'm just going to stop there. This is what we were just talking about, your representative asserted as part of these proceedings before the Human Rights Chamber; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The decision goes on to state: "Further, he claims that he has 'reliable information' about his accusation. The applicant did not disclose this information and has failed to provide the Chamber with any evidence." The next paragraph then rejects this accusation as manifestly ill-founded. The fact is you had no support for your conspiracy theory; right?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Objection --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: -- especially if he is relying upon this document since the document itself has contradictory information in another part of it. So is he relying upon the document as a whole or in that one paragraph?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, I take it you will deal with that in re-examination, but already, Mr. Weber, you know what to expect -- if you have taken out of context the portion, then you know what happens, and if you want to anticipate on that, of course you may do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The fact is that the Chamber, as it says here, rejected the applicant's complaint about the lack of impartiality of one of the judges. That's what that decision was?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Correct. But I don't know why we are talking about the second judgement. Why doesn't the Prosecutor show you the first judgement of the Human Rights Chamber which provides a very detailed account of the entire case because this judgement and the second proceedings before the Human Rights Chamber was conducted after I was released and after we applied for a re-trial. We wanted everything to start from scratch and that new facts would be taken into account; however, we were not granted that leave.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, please focus on my question. Is it correct that since 2008 [sic] you've been making claims that there was this big conspiracy, where everyone from the trial judge in your initial proceedings before the cantonal court who found you guilty, to your own lawyers who were defending you and presenting an alibi that you were in Tuzla during Herenda's interview, to the prosecutor who was seeking a conviction for your mistreatment of Herenda during the interview --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE FLUEGGE
utterances.text: You should slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: To even a Supreme Court judge and your former co-workers were all collaborating to not have your story about Herenda's interview come out. That's what you've been claiming since 1998, right, since your initial conviction was upheld?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, your recorded as initially referring to "since 2008" and now "since 1998."

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you for the clarification. I meant since 1998 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: -- when his original conviction was upheld.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: That's clear. Could you please answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Besides confusing 2008 and 1998, the Prosecutor obviously confused two different judgements of the Human Rights Chamber. I stand by the first judgement which was passed in 2000. The second judgement in 2002 is not relevant at all. I just wanted to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Witness, would you please focus on the question. The question was whether you claimed since 1998 what Mr. Weber told us, not to further explain about this judgement, but whether those were the claims you made.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Correct. Since 1998, since the month of September of that year, I have firmly stood by my assertion and I'm repeating it today.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You and your two colleagues maltreated Herenda while he was in your custody; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 12 of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In paragraph 71 of the Human Rights Chamber's 2002 decision it states: "The Chamber recalls that the Supreme Court established that the applicant 'hit the injured party'" in reference to Herenda "'with his fist, bound him to the pipe of the radiator, inserted a wooden club between his hands when he was already cuffed and hit him on different parts of his body.' The Supreme Court further stated that 'the injured party was subject to physical and psychical harm' and thereby assessed that 'these actions fulfil the characteristics of maltreatment in discharge of duty.'" The fact is you were found guilty of maltreating Herenda; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: In order to understand this, you have to know how the Human Rights Chamber functioned. The way it functioned was --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir -- sir --

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: -- that both sides lodged their appeals in order to make their positions known. Now what you are --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The fact is the Human Rights Chamber upheld your conviction for maltreatment in the discharge of duty; right? Simple question.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Not right. The Human Rights Chamber did not uphold it, but rather it did not order the case to be sent for re-trial. But it didn't uphold the original judgement. It dropped the whole thing. And what you just read is a quote from the rigged indictment that the Supreme Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina tried to defend twice and owing to your colleagues from the Prosecutor, Mr. Kenning more precisely, that didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Weber, I announced that I was not available --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: -- and I think, as a matter of fact, that my colleagues would prefer to take the break now, then to resume at ten minutes past 1.00 and then to inform you whether they have decided or not decided to continue to hear the case, and then if they would have decided to do so, to continue until quarter past 2.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. Just to have a fully clean break, is there any way I could please tender this document into evidence? It's 65 ter 31923.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7279, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Admitted into evidence. Witness, we'll take a break of 20 minutes. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Usually I say "we resume," but the court resumes at ten minutes past 1.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: May the witness please be escorted into the courtroom. In the meantime, I just wanted to say that Judge Orie may not have mentioned it but it is important to place on the record that he's not with us this afternoon due to urgent personal business. As a result, Judge Fluegge and I have decided, in the interests of justice, to carry on with the trial. And as a result, therefore, we are going to be sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis of the Rules of Procedure and Evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Before we carry on, Mr. Weber, how much more time do you think you will need?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to approximate an hour. I'm trying to keep the witness focused on his answers but they've gone a little long. So I do have some material to go through, but I will finish by the end of the day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: So we're not likely to finish this afternoon?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I don't know if there's redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Well, if you're going for an hour, it will be an hour by the time we finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I'm going to try to finish today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Ivetic, at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Right now only a few questions, two or three questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. You may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, during these proceedings in this case - and what I'm going to be referring to can be found at transcript page 20096, lines 23 to 25 - the Defence claimed that Mr. Herenda was kidnapped and tortured by his colleagues. The Prosecution does not dispute the fact that you and two of your colleagues took Mr. Herenda and tortured him. That is what happened, you and your colleagues tortured Herenda while he was in your custody; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: This is not correct. We treated Herenda in keeping with our authorities. Later, in the reprocess it was construed that we had tortured Herenda in order to gain financial gain, i.e., 500 German marks, a Zippo lighter, and a silver necklace. That was the financial gain we were supposed to gain from allegedly kidnapping him.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Herenda sustained severe injuries during his time with you; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Nedzad Herenda sustained injuries during his flight attempt. In the re-trial, the colleague who was with me who prevented that escape confirmed that he did not sustain any injuries from torture. His leg was injured when he tried to snatch a gun and use it in his flight attempt.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: That was it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That was it.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Herenda, in fact, was shot and beaten while he was in your custody; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Herenda was not beaten; however, when he was fighting for the gun or the pistol, the pistol fired and wounded him in the leg. As he was trying to escape, he sustained a head blow. Later on, this was construed as an attempt to shoot into his head.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 31918 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Coming up before you are excerpts from the 13 June 1997 judgement of the Sarajevo Cantonal Court against you, Haris Pezo, and Refik Muran. I would just like to go through some of the evidence that was presented during your original trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 8 of the B/C/S original and page 7 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, I'd like to direct your attention to the lower middle of the page where it discusses the material that was available to the medical expert in the trial. According to the judgement, this material included Herenda's medical records from the Kosevo Hospital, the emergency medical centre in Sarajevo; a neurologist's report; x-rays of Herenda's leg and head; and a CT scan. Then if I could direct you toward the bottom of the page where it states: "On the basis of the available medical documentation" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: "... Expert Witness Dobraca ultimately reported that several injuries were in evidence on the injured party's body, some of which were minor and others serious. He noted there were two areas of soft tissue damage in the parietal-occipital region of the head consisting of two wounds limited to the soft tissue of the scalp which are therefore minor injuries. However, the CT scan and the testimony of Witness Sulejmanpasic indicated that one of these injuries also included the fracturing of the parietal and occipital bonds on the right side and the injury qualified by Expert Witness Dobraca is a serious bodily injury. Interpretation of the CT scan showed that one of several features of the injured party's two head wounds included a skull fracture. Having been informed of the results of the analysis of the ballistics expert, that metal debris found in the skin of the injured party's scalp were parts of bullet rounds." Sir, the truth is that Herenda sustained serious injuries to the head during the interview as a result of a gun-shot; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Not correct. You're quoting from the judgement which resulted from the rigged proceedings in the year 2002, when we decided to remain silent and when the corrupted panel tried to hush up the role of Herenda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- and the crimes that he had committed --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, let me stop you. Whether the judgement was rigged or not, that is immaterial. That is what is written in the judgement; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- that was part of the judgement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. That was the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: On page 2 of this decision, which is also on the bottom of page 2 in the B/C/S, the court found that the injuries suffered by Herenda included the serious bodily harm of fracture of the temporal and occipital bones, a number of less serious bodily injuries, consisting of haematomas, and scratches on the skin of the face, arms, the chest below the right breast, front side of the abdomen, left side of the chest, and left lower leg. The truth is Herenda was beaten and shot during your three-day-long interview and sustained multiple injuries to different areas of his body; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: This is based on the report of expert Dobraca who himself was a Seve member. You can find that in previous documents and statements. This is not correct because we treated Herenda --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to stop you, sir. You keep criticising and commenting on the quality of the evidence given. That's not the question. The question is that what is being read to you is what is in that judgement. Now, whether Dobraca was part of the Seve or not is not the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, actually, the question by the Prosecution was not as Your Honour had said. He's actually asking the question that the witness is answering, so I would take exception to that characterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. In that event, then you may carry on, Mr. Weber.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At this time the Prosecution tenders 65 ter 31918 into evidence. It's excerpts from the judgement. We've reduced the size of it to the relevant parts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: 31918 is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7280, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'd like to change topics with you and discuss your evidence related to the death of Sefer Halilovic's wife. First I'd like to look at your previous testimony regarding this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have D980, page 17. Okay. If we could scroll down just towards the middle of the page.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is another part of your testimony in the Karadzic case. During this examination you were asked: "And how was this presented to General Halilovic, and what was the public told? What was the official position on this matter?" You answered: "The public was told that this was a shell launched by the Serbian Army, or the Army of Republika Srpska, that it was a guided projectile of the Maljutka type, as far as I can recall from Herenda's statement, because he and the other perpetrators left a Maljutka wire, which is a characteristic of that particular projectile. They left that behind in order to create the impression that this was a Maljutka launched from Serb positions." You describe a projectile, a Maljutka. This is a type of rocket-propelled anti-tank missile; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I'm not a ballistics expert. I suppose so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The closest Serbian position to the north of the Halilovic residence was several kilometres away from their place; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I believe that it was not so much away because the closest position near the Jezero hospital were about 1 kilometre as the crow flies and Halilovic's apartment was in the part of the city known as Ciglane, brickworks.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Do you know that Maljutkas have a firing range of up to 2800 metres, which in this instance would make it a weapon that would not likely have come from Serb positions? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I object to the question as it mixes up the evidence based upon the distances that we've just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think it's a perfectly phrased question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not -- I don't understand that basis, Mr. Ivetic. Because it mixes up the evidence upon the distances that we've just discussed.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: We've been talking about kilometres and now we're talking about 2800 metres according to the transcript. So to say that it's beyond the range of the weapon is not accurate, where we've just had the evidence that 1 kilometre, which would be 1.000 metres in my understanding, so it would be within the range of the weapon. So to state that the fact that the rocket has a range of 2800 metres eliminates it from being a potential used -- it misstates the evidence we've just heard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the position of the Prosecution is that it was 3 kilometres away which would make it 3.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Then he should phrase the question that way, Your Honour. That's not the question that he asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I put the question fine to the witness. It is our position what I asked, so I would like to hear his answer on the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic would like you to state based on your position not based on -- his says it was a mile away, you say it was 3 miles away.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, our position is that the Maljutkas have a firing range of up to 2800 metres, and based on the actual distance between where the residence was and the closest Serb positions that it would have unlikely come from the Serb side; right? Are you aware of this?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I believe that there is some confusion here. Herenda admitted that an explosive was planted and that it killed General Halilovic's wife and brother, and then it was made believe that it was Maljutka. A wire was left there just to make believe that it was Maljutka. But what happened was that they planted explosives which they activated from the building across the road. When they realised that Halilovic's wife and her brother came out on to the balcony, at that moment when they saw them, they actually thought that Mrs. Halilovic's brother was Mr. Halilovic himself. That's when they activated the explosive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: You really didn't answer my question, but I'm going to move along. I appreciate that you're not a ballistics expert, but do you realise that a Maljutka is a different type of projectile than an artillery shell fired from a howitzer?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I'm telling you again, I'm not an expert in ballistics, but I know it was mentioned that an explosive device was set up. There was no talk about a projectile or any other detail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: So that's the extent of your knowledge; is that what you're saying? That just a statement was made to you and that's it?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Then it's correct that you did not check any fire tables or conduct any ballistics measurements which may or may not indicate an artillery shell from a 122-millimetre howitzer impacted the balcony area? You're not aware of any of that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's right, because we were arrested immediately after the interview with Herenda --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, you've answered --

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: -- and we had no authority. It was not in our purview to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, I'm going to try and finish with you today. If you could please just focus on my questions. The explosion that killed General Halilovic's wife and associate occurred on 7 July 1993. Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In your previous testimony, you claim that Herenda told you he planted an explosive to eliminate General Halilovic because, a couple months beforehand, General Halilovic had been removed from his authority over the ABiH and Herenda understood him to be an enemy of the state, at least according to what Herenda told you. Are you aware that Alija Izetbegovic relieved Sefer Halilovic of his duties as Chief of the Main Staff of the ABiH on 1 November 1993, after the death of his wife?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I don't know that, but Herenda said that he had received an assignment from Ugljen to eliminate Halilovic by setting up an explosive device on his balcony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have 65 ter 32369 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: This is the 16 April 1999 decision of the Sarajevo cantonal prosecutor's office which dismissed the criminal complaint of Sefer Halilovic related to the event that we've been discussing on 7 July 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 2 of both versions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: In the top paragraph before you, which is the second paragraph in the statement of reasons section, the decision indicates that the support for the allegations was based on a hearing and an interview with you. There is then a number of articles listed from "Slobodna Bosna" and "Dani" from September and October 1998. These articles contained interviews or statements from you; correct? These were the newspapers that you provided interviews to in September and October of 1998; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: No, these journalists received my statements that I had forwarded to the Human Rights Chamber and then they published it, I don't know through which channels. I see this document for the first time. And I see that it was issued by the cantonal prosecution office that rigged my trial in 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have page 3 of the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At the end of the next paragraph, the decision states that the official reports of the forensic commission and of the experts for ballistics from 7 July, the date of the incident, 20 and 31 July 1993, claimed beyond any doubt that the individuals at the residence were killed by an artillery projectile which came from the direction of the enemy positions from Vogosca. This is in fact what happened. The artillery -- there was an artillery projectile fired from Vogosca and that's why these charges were dismissed; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I stress again, I am seeing this document for the first time, and as far as I know, right now there is a re-trial going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina trying to establish whether things happened the way I described it or it was a shell from enemy positions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Prosecution tendered this document into evidence, 65 ter 32369.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit P7281, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would like now to discuss with you the shooting of the French member of UNPROFOR. In your past testimony, you commented upon the document that indicated this event occurred on the 15th of April, 1995. This document was admitted with your testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could the Prosecution please have Exhibit P3, e-court page 25 for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I would like to go through some of the things that you've said about this event.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And if we could please have the photograph on the right-hand side. Great. And if we could just slide down a little bit and zoom-out one time, please. So if we could have the yellow building, the Holiday Inn, and the buildings on the lower side of the river visible, that would be great. Perfect. Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, you recognise the area depicted in the photograph; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I recognise this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: If the court usher could please assist the Prosecution with -- or the witness with a pen to mark on the photograph.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: At transcript page 33388 of your Karadzic testimony, you indicated that Herenda supposedly told you he fired from the Executive Council building. Could you please mark the location of this building with the letter E.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: It's not true, nor did we specify exactly where it came from, but I suppose it's this large building here. He didn't say exactly. Now it houses the Executive Council of ministers and the Parliament building, but he didn't tell us the exact position in his statement, nor did we ask him for the exact position. But the very fact that he shot an international observer astounded us, so we didn't look into the details.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: The Executive Council building was located in the area under control of the ABiH army throughout the war; right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Right. This is the separation line, that's the river --

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, if you can hold off making any markings on the document. I see that you've made a horizontal line where the river is to denote where the separation line was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And could that line be please deleted.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry. [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: I see you've marked with a circle the general area where you believe Herenda told you he was at. In your 2000 interview with the OTP, you indicated that the French soldier was hit across the way or opposite the Holiday Inn on a crossroads where there is a museum. Is this right?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Could you please mark the approximate location where the French soldier was hit with the number 1.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Well, now I don't know exactly which location it is, whether it's this intersection or this one. There is an intersection here and there's the second one here, and this is the hotel, Holiday Inn. So these two intersections are on the two sides of Holiday Inn. But I'm telling you we did not ask for the exact position.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, and I can show this to you if you want, you indicated previously that that occurred across the way or opposite the Holiday Inn on a crossroads where there is a museum. Do you remember saying this? That would be -- what you previously said, that would be where location number 2 is at; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: If I may mark, this is the museum and this is Holiday Inn, so both intersections are across the street from Holiday Inn. I can't tell you which of the two it is because I'm telling you at that time we didn't look for the details. We just dealt with the fact that he committed this murder.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Now, is it right that Herenda supposedly told you that he climbed up to one of the upper floors of the Executive Council building to fire from?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I can't tell you with any certainty from which position he fired. I only know that he mentioned the building of these two joint institutions, the Executive Council and the Parliament. One building is lower than the other, six floors versus 15.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honours, could I have one moment, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You may.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Sir, Mr. Herenda didn't tell you that the Executive Council building where he was at or that area was fired upon after the UNPROFOR soldier was shot; correct?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: I can't remember exactly whether he was exposed to fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: Your Honour, just so we have a complete record, the witness marked with an H the location of the Holiday Inn and an M the location of the museum. With that, the Prosecution would tender this document as marked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The document as marked is admitted into evidence. May it please be given an exhibit number, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P7282, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: And with that, Your Honours, I have no further questions for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Weber. Mr. Ivetic, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honours, it will be brief. If we could first turn to the prior testimony, D980, page 23 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: While we wait for that, a Dr. Dobraca was mentioned by the Prosecution in relation to the testimony as to Mr. Herenda's alleged injuries and you indicated that a doctor -- that that was the doctor who had been part of the Seve. If we can wait for the part of the transcript that we're waiting for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Ivetic, while we're waiting for it, can I interrupt you a little bit?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I've just been made aware of the fact that P7281 was not properly admitted. It is hereby admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Sir, in this part of your testimony in the Karadzic case you're talking about a pathologist, Ilijas Dobraca, whose job was to provide medical certificates after certain assassinations to cover them up. Is this the same Dr. Dobraca that provided the medical information purporting to show Mr. Herenda's injuries resulting from the interview?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: That's correct. There was only one doctor named Ilija Dobraca.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, in answer to the Prosecution's question where they said: Isn't it true that Herenda was beaten and shot during the three-day interview with multiple injuries as confirmed by Dr. Dobraca, you were not allowed to answer the question fully. I would like to give you the opportunity to complete your answer as to the Prosecution's assertion that Mr. Herenda was beaten and shot during the three-day interview with multiple injuries therefrom.

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: The very order we received said it was a dangerous armed criminal, and when he was bound and handcuffed, certainly it left traces on his arms. During the arrest and his treatment, we followed the law governing the agency and it's not true what the trumped-up indictment said. But during his attempt to escape, Herenda took advantage of a moment of inattention by Haris who was guarding him, tried to seize his weapon, and it resulted in him being injured in the leg. After that, we turned him over to Mr. Fikret Masic, who was to treat his injury. But even before that, we bandaged his leg and thus provided him with emergency medical assistance before turning him over to the doctor.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And I'd like to now look at P7279, which was also used during the cross-examination, and to start off I'd like to look at page 3 of the same.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: This will be the 2002 decision on admissibility and merits of the Human Rights Chamber for Bosnia-Herzegovina, and I'd like to look at paragraph 17 of the same, which states: "On 5 October 2000, the applicant also challenged Judge Malik Hadziomeragic on the grounds of partiality due to the allegation that he was in contact with the secret service AID (Agencija za istrazvanje i dokumentaciju). The applicant explained before the Supreme Court panel that persons from the AID told him during the first set of the proceedings that the dispute would be solved positively due to the collaboration of the mentioned judge with the AID. He complained that, contrary to the promise, the result was not positive. On the same day, 5 October 2000, the president of the Supreme Court decided to reject the applicant's challenge propter affectum as ill-founded due to the lack of evidence in support of the motion and on any other indication of partiality." And now that the translation is finished, the question I have for you, sir, is: First of all, does this accurately describe the fact that the Chamber decided the same day as you gave them all this information to dismiss the allegation of partiality on the part of the stated judge, Hadziomeragic?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: As far as I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And in relation to your complaints about the judge, did another organisation also present a report about the same in support of your appeal?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes, Amnesty International cited my trial as an example of a rigged trial and an example of a violation of human rights. They actively followed it all the time, from 1998, when I first appealed to the Human Rights Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: For Your Honours' reference, on the next page, paragraph 22 discusses Amnesty International's position. Since this has been entered into evidence, we don't need to have that read. I'd like to now turn to page 14 of this exhibit, and I'd like to focus on section 2.2. And the bottom of this page is signed Giovanni Grasso, and in 2.2, it says as follows: "In the present case the fear of the applicant as to the impartiality of the Court appears to be fully reasonable and justified because not only some but all the judges who decided upon the renewed appeal had already decided upon the previous appeal, taking a clear position on his criminal responsibility after an evaluation of all the circumstances of the case. The subject matter of the renewed appeal proceedings and of the original proceedings was exactly the same, so that the impartiality of the judges who had already taken a decision on the case is clearly open to doubts." At temporary transcript page 52, lines 20 to 24, you indicated a dissent of Mr. Grasso. Is this the dissent that you're talking about?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And for purposes of the record, could you please tell us who Mr. Grasso was, what position he held?

utterances.speaker: EDIN GARAPLIJA
utterances.text: Mr. Grasso presided over the Human Rights Chamber in the first proceedings, otherwise he is an Italian judge as far as I know. There were a total of six international judges from different countries.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Garaplija, thank you for answering my questions and for your time today.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, that completes my redirect.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivetic. Nothing arising, Mr. Weber?

utterances.speaker: MR. WEBER
utterances.text: No, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Mr. Garaplija, that concludes your testimony before the Tribunal. I want to thank you very much for coming all the way to come and answer the questions, and we wish you a safe return back home. You may follow the usher.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Is the Defence ready to call the next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: No, we are not, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. LUKIC
utterances.text: We had -- probably you were informed that we had some technical problems with this witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We just wanted to have it on the record that we don't have one. Thank you so much. In that event, we will stand adjourned, and we will reconvene tomorrow morning at 9.30 in the morning in the same courtroom, I. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 1st day of April, 2015, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
